alt: The booth before dawn. Ray, the lead engineer, welcomes Maya — a new volunteer on her first Sunday on headset.
Four colored lines — signal, power, control, network — flow through the booth between Ray and Maya.
Flashback: a laptop shows the livestream stuck on BUFFERING. Maya throws her hands up, wondering what she broke.
Ray points to a chart of the seven network layers, stacked like floors of a building: 1 physical at the bottom up to 7 application at the top.
Soundcheck on stage: two microphones on stands, the digital console glowing, Maya waiting at the desk.
The meters light up red from the preamp onward — the signal is clipping. 'CRRK!' Maya jumps back from the console.
Ray points to the meters: every stage now sits in the green, from the microphone to the fader.
Ray points at four colored lanes — the vocal, drum, music and speech buses — that forty channels feed into.
Maya saves the console scene; the screen reads SCENE SAVED — SUNDAY 01. Ray nods.
The sanctuary seen through a murky blue haze, like the sound is underwater.
Ray points to an analyzer graph with a big hump between 250 and 500 hertz, shaded red.
An EQ curve shows a gentle cut around 350 hertz. Maya and Ray listen.
A side view of the room: a center-fill loudspeaker tilted up at the ceiling. Its sound reaches seat 13 twice — directly, and late after bouncing off the ceiling.
A graph of the sound at seat 13 swings between sharp peaks and deep nulls — comb filtering. Ray explains.
The fill loudspeaker is re-aimed flat at the listeners; a green check mark. Maya points at the seats.
A mixer and a laptop connected by an audio cable. Each is plugged into a different outlet; a dashed red loop runs between their grounds. A low HMMMMM fills the room.
The same diagram, labeled: two paths to ground make a loop. Ray explains from the side.
Fixed: the mixer and the laptop now share one power strip — one ground, one system — with every safety earth left connected.
A camera points at the LED wall; on camera the wall shows pink rippling bands. Maya frowns at it.
Two readouts side by side: the camera at 59.94 and the LED wall at 59.94 — matched. Ray points; Maya grins.
9:58. Maya's finger hovers over a big pink GO LIVE button on the streaming laptop.
Ray holds up the pre-stream checklist, every box ticked: audio, video, stream key, return feed, backup recording.
The sanctuary is full and the LIVE light is on. Maya and Ray stand in the booth doorway.
Three fixtures cross their beams on the stage: warm key from one side, cool fill from the other, a pink back light from above.
A top-view diagram: the subject in the middle, a key light at 45 degrees, a fill light opposite, a back light behind. Maya explains.
After the service, Ray holds the debrief card — what broke, what almost broke, what to fix before next week. Maya listens.
The empty sanctuary in warm light. Maya stands in the aisle, proud.
Closing: the sanctuary full and warm; Maya and Ray stand together at the back, the machinery forgotten.
Flashback: a phone shows the livestream frozen on Pastor Jo mid-gesture with a spinning buffering wheel. Chat messages read 'Frozen again?' and 'We lost you, Pastor — Ms. Evelyn'.
Flashback in the booth: Maya's hands hover over the stream computer, frozen with worry, while Imani reaches under the desk and pulls the power on a small network switch.
Early morning in the church parking lot. Maya sits in her car with cold coffee and her headset around her neck, looking at the building like it might bite.
In the booth, Ray labels a cable. His mug is labeled too: RAY — NOT DECAF. Maya stands in the doorway.
Ray holds out a white cable tie to Maya.
Theo, a volunteer in his early twenties, backs through the door carrying a cardboard box marked MISC CABLES (GOOD ONES), grinning.
Imani, the technical director, passes the booth and checks in with Maya, who answers too quickly.
A sticky note on the stream computer's monitor reads DO NOT UPDATE ON SUNDAY. An update prompt sits just under it. Maya eyes it like a suspect.
Ray pulls a stool over and doesn't sit on it. He talks to Maya.
Maya glances at the stream computer as she answers Ray.
Ray traces four things with one finger. In System View, four faint lines bloom over the booth, labeled SIGNAL, POWER, CONTROL and NETWORK. Maya writes the four words in her notebook.
At the lighting desk, Sofia calls over about the haze drifting across the stage.
Walking the center aisle during soundcheck, Maya pauses in the middle rows and tilts her head.

On the booth phone, the private test stream's waveform shows gaps: the sound drops out for a second or two while the picture keeps moving. Maya's hand moves toward the restart button. A confidence tick beside her reads 90.
Ray asks Maya how confident she is.
Ray asks what would change her mind. Maya has no answer.

Maya walks the four paths: every power light is on, the console's stream meters are steady, the stream settings are unchanged, and the little switch under the desk has every light flickering hard and feels warm. She adds 'heat? ENVIRONMENT' to her notebook.
The stream computer's own network monitor shows it receiving hundreds of megabits per second when the stream needs only a few. Maya's confidence that the computer is at fault drops from 90 to 30.
Ray leans in toward the console. Maya notices the dropouts pause whenever he leans in.

Ray's inventory photo from last month shows the switch with three cables. Today it has five, including a new blue one. On the back of the switch, facing the wall, a faded label: TEMP — AUDIO + STREAM ONLY — M.
Maya follows the new blue cable out of the switch, through the floor box, into the equipment room, to a patch panel with a sticky note that says 'overflow!!'.
Theo appears in the equipment-room doorway, glowing with pride.
Maya speaks warmly to Theo.
Flashback, from Theo's point of view: Saturday, the empty fellowship hall. A donated video encoder and decoder; the camera picture on the big screen, perfect. He leaves a sticky note.
Theo, quieter now, admits something. Maya goes still.
Maya's notebook: 'Last week: same cause? SUSPECTED. Can't prove it — the switch was restarted.' Ray stands beside her.
Theo does the arithmetic out loud, stricken.
Imani, Ray, Theo and Maya crowd into the booth. Imani asks for one sentence.
Imani asks about the overflow room.
In the equipment room, another switch — the church office's — has open ports. Maya looks at it.

A teaching moment: Ray and Maya beside a board. Signal flow is the path from the source to the people — every box in between. Tonight the path ran through a switch that was full. How full is full? Utilization: traffic divided by link speed, times a hundred. Ninety megabits on a hundred-megabit port is ninety percent. A jammed hallway.
Priya answers her phone in her kitchen, a plate of pancakes on the counter and a child negotiating in the background.
Priya gives her recommendation over the phone.
Imani decides.
Imani speaks to everyone; Theo raises his hand to set up the lobby TV before anyone asks.
Ray asks for a prediction before Maya pulls the cable.
Maya states her prediction with a confidence tick of 75.
Close-up: one hand unplugs one blue network cable from the switch. In System View the crowded traffic lane thins to a trickle; the receive rate falls; the switch is exactly as warm as before.
Maya reaches for her pen to write FIXED. Ray stops her with a question.
Ray asks who they were doing this for. Maya is already grabbing her phone and heading for the door.
Proof panel S01E00-P014-PN03. The parking lot: Wi-Fi off, cellular on, earbuds in, phone at arm's length, a ten-minute timer. Families arrive in their good clothes. Ray's voice on the radio.
Behind Maya, the church doors open at 9:12. She writes in her notebook.

Back inside, Maya checks what she might have broken: the pastor's mic check from the front, middle and back rows is fine, the console tablet is still in control, and the lobby TV has picture and sound a few seconds behind, as Imani accepted.
The stream goes live. Maya says the line this time, and means it.
10:41 on the booth clock. Everyone looks at the clock except Ray, who looks at Maya. She has the stream on her phone, on cellular, in one ear.
At a distance and in silhouette: Pastor Jo baptizes Lily. The congregation watches.
Theo's phone buzzes and he holds it out to Maya. A text from Walter: 'I can see her. Clear as day. Tell Maya thank you.' Maya can't say anything at all.
11:40, the debrief. Imani asks the three questions.
Maya answers carefully.
Maya continues, looking at Theo.
A blank sheet headed in Ray's handwriting: BOOTH CHANGE LOG. Maya writes the first entry. Theo adds Saturday's, after the fact.
Imani opens a problem record for last Sunday. Maya writes UNKNOWN beside last week in her notebook.

Maya's printed label wrapped on the blue cable: OVERFLOW ENC — TEMPORARY — SEE LOG #1. On the desk, Ray's old notebook lies open to a page the reader can see and Maya can't: 'console pw' followed by a blacked-out password.
Ray on the phone with Mateo, whose voice we only hear.
Maya threads the morning's cable tie onto her lanyard. End card: SIGNAL.
From Dolores's seat in row 8: Pastor Jo preaching at the front. The words arrive thin and doubled, like a voice down a hallway.
Dolores, 81, leans forward in her pew and adjusts her hearing aid. She leans further.
An usher kneels beside Dolores holding out an assistive listening receiver. She waves it away, too quickly, and looks at her hands.
After the service, in the aisle, Dolores's daughter Ana speaks quietly to Imani. Maya, coiling a cable nearby, stops.
Maya's notebook from last week, three words: 'center — kind of hollow.' Maya, under her breath.

The empty sanctuary on Tuesday evening. Up in the booth, Priya photographs every cable for the network drawing she promised. Maya and Ray walk the center aisle while last Sunday's sermon recording plays.
At row 8 the voice goes hollow for Maya too. She steps one seat left; it changes. One more; it changes again.
Ray sits in the back row with a cup of coffee, reading, like a man with nowhere to be.
Maya stops herself before touching anything.
Maya walks all ten seats with a measurement microphone taped to a broom handle, recording each seat before touching anything. Ray, still reading, doesn't look up.

Two years of comment cards from the usher drawer, spread on the booth desk. Maya marks each complaint on a seating chart. A tight cluster appears: rows 7 to 9, center. A few stray cards are about other things.
Maya pulls up the renovation photos from the shared drive: a new center-fill loudspeaker hung above the platform lip, tilted up toward the balcony front.
Maya lists four explanations out loud. Ray, still reading, turns a page.

Four small panels, one per test: the microphone — the same recording is clean in every other seat, contradicted; Dolores's hearing — Maya hears it too, so it isn't only Dolores, contradicted as the cause of the room problem; air handling — switched off and on, no change, contradicted; the room — fill alone clear, mains alone clear, both together hollow, suspected.

System View: for the first time, two lines to the same seat — a short solid line from the main loudspeakers and a longer dashed one from the fill that goes up to the ceiling and comes back down, each tagged with when it arrives: early, late.
Two analyzer strips, seat 12 and seat 13, labeled ANALYZER. Both show a row of notches, but the notches sit at different frequencies from one seat to the next.

A teaching moment: Ray and Maya beside a board. A comb filter is the same sound arriving twice, a hair apart. Some frequencies cancel. Each cancelled one is a notch. Where's the first notch? One over twice the gap. Arrivals one millisecond apart: one divided by two thousandths — five hundred hertz.

Maya's whiteboard drawing: the fill, the ceiling, and a mirror image of the fill above the ceiling. A straight dotted line from the mirror image to seat 13 shows the reflection's true path; the red dashed reflected path is longer than the green direct path from the mains.

The whiteboard numbers: delta L about 1.7 meters; delta t equals delta L over c, about 1.7 meters divided by 343 meters per second, about 4.96 milliseconds; first notch near 101 hertz, then every 202 hertz; seat 12, delta L about 1.4 meters, notches near 123 hertz and every 245 hertz. Illustrative geometry.
Maya states what would prove her wrong before she tests it.
Before and after: seat 13's analyzer strip with the fill turned down 6 decibels. The notches get shallower. The hollowness softens but doesn't vanish.
Ray finally closes his book and asks Maya a question.
The fill loudspeaker hangs three meters up on an overhead mount, tilted toward the ceiling. Maya looks up at it from the floor.
Maya calls Mateo, who installed the fill. His voice on speaker.
Mateo offers to bring a lift.
Wednesday lunchtime. Maya's phone rings: it's Ana.
Maya takes a breath and says only what she knows.
Maya continues, and Ana is quiet, then answers.

Thursday. Mateo on the lift re-aiming the fill; a crew member below; yellow tape ropes off the area with a sign reading NO ONE UNDER THE LOAD. Maya stays outside the tape with her broom-handle microphone.
The fill is re-aimed down at the middle rows, at ear height. Mateo photographs the new angle and signs the work record.

Maya's measurements after the re-aim: the ten seats' deep notches are gone; four side seats are still covered; the balcony front is noticeably weaker than before. She writes it down rather than hiding it.
During the sermon Maya slips into an empty seat at the end of row 8 and listens: a full room and a live voice. No hollowness.
Dolores in her seat. Halfway through the sermon, she sits back.
After the service Dolores finds Maya in the booth.
Change log entry #2: 'Center fill re-aimed (Mateo, Thursday). Trim back to 0 dB. Balcony front now weaker — owner decision needed.' Imani adds it to her budget list.
Ray reads the change-log entry.

Late on a Tuesday, Priya and Maya run a controlled test: the overflow encoder, now on its own small switch, is plugged back into the old booth switch for sixty seconds. The receive rate jumps and the test stream drops audio; unplugged, it recovers.
Maya updates the pilot's incident note: the mechanism is verified by controlled reproduction; last Sunday's freeze is still unknown.
A wide, muted view of the sanctuary during a song. The worship leader, Marisol, sings; the band plays; the sound feels heavy.
Maya at the console with a tablet analyzer, clearly labeled ANALYZER, showing a broad bump shaded between 250 and 500 hertz.
Close-up: Maya cuts a dip in the EQ between 250 and 500 hertz. Then, almost without thinking, her hand nudges the main fader up.
Maya grins: 'Better.' The congregation sings. In the corner of the panel, the channel 1 input meter's red clip light flickers on the chorus. Maya doesn't see it.
Theo drops his sister Lily off at the booth. She has come to learn the board.
Maya teaches Lily at the console, pointing at the input meters.
Maya answers, a little too fast.
The band starts. The sound is heavy again. Maya explains the mud; Lily asks why.
Maya gives the rule. Lily keeps asking.
Maya opens her mouth, then closes it. Her notebook: 'Mud = 250–500. Cut it. WORKED.' Below it she writes: 'WHY did it work?'
Maya listens in headphones to one channel at a time: drums fine, keys fine, guitar a little heavy, and the lead vocal, on the choruses, heavy.
Dante arrives: tall, bronze bomber jacket, short locs, in-ear protection visible. He holds out foam earplugs to Maya and Lily.
Dante listens with his head tilted, eyes closed, one hand cupped behind his ear. In System View, his listening is a focused cone on one frequency region.
Teach-back: Maya explains her recipe to Dante.
Close-up: a worn sticker on Dante's audio interface reads MATCH FIRST.
Maya and Lily close their eyes and face away from the console while Dante switches between two versions of Sunday's recording: A is Maya's cut, B is flat.
Round one result card: Maya picks her cut 5 times out of 5. Dante reaches for his sound-level meter.
Round two, with the loudness matched: Maya picks the cut 5 times out of 10, Lily 4 out of 10 — no better than chance.
Round three: Dante tests his own favorite 'warm' setting on the acoustic guitar, blind and level-matched. He picks it 3 times out of 6. He laughs.
Lily asks where the heaviness comes from, if not the EQ. Maya remembers a field note: fix problems at the earliest stage you can reach.

A teaching moment: Ray and Maya beside a board. Gain is how much a stage adds, in decibels. Gain staging is setting every stage so the signal sits clear of the noise and clear of clipping. And how much gain do I add? Target minus what arrives. Arriving at minus thirty, you want minus eighteen: minus eighteen minus minus thirty — plus twelve. Headroom is what's left above your peaks.
Maya watches the channel 1 input meter while Marisol sings the chorus. The red clip light lights on every chorus peak.
System View: the signal chain — mic, preamp, EQ, fader, room and stream. The preamp box is red: clipping happens there, before the EQ.
Maya asks who set the gain. Lily reads Sunday's line-check sheet.
Maya puts it together.
On stage, Marisol sings the chorus with her lips almost touching the mic grille, then backs away for the verse. Dante explains.
System View: two bar charts. Up close to the microphone, the low-frequency bar is much taller than the others; a hand's width back, the bars even out. Illustrative.
Maya's notebook: 'Too much gain for how she really sings, so it clips on choruses. Close to the mic, extra lows. EQ comes after both.' Confidence: 70.
Dante asks for a prediction before Maya touches anything.
Close-up: Maya turns the preamp gain knob down. The input meter now peaks below the red on the chorus. Dante matches the loudness with his sound-level meter.
Maya listens again. Better — but something is left.
On stage, Maya shows Marisol the input meter on a tablet while Lily watches.
Marisol watches the meter change as she moves and laughs.
Lily rewrites the line-check sheet: 'Sing the loudest line, at the real distance.'
Round four, blind and level-matched: tonight's version against Sunday's. Maya picks tonight's 9 of 10, Lily 9 of 10, Dante 10 of 10. Illustrative.
Sunday, during the service: through every chorus, channel 1's input meter stays out of the red. The clip log shows zero events. Illustrative.
Maya walks to the middle of the room during a song and listens. In row 8, Dolores sits back, singing.
Adjacent checks: the pastor's mic is clear from the front, middle and back rows; the stream recording shows no clipping, and its level is close to last week's.
After the service, Dante plays last week's stream recording against this week's, loudness matched.
Maya asks Lily to teach it back to her.

Maya's notebook rewrites the old field note: '250 to 500 hertz is a place to look, not a rule — it depends on the voice and the room. Match the level before you judge. Fix it at the earliest stage you can reach.'
Change log entry #3: 'Channel 1 (lead vocal) preamp gain lowered. Scene saved. Line check now at singing level, real distance. Blind A/B results attached.'
Ray reads the entry and gives one principle.
Dante notices a sticky note on the console with the password on it. He asks Ray about it. Ray pauses.
Imani passes the booth with news. Maya glances at the drawer of adapters.
Imani brings the guest speaker, Dr. Naomi Park, to the booth. Dr. Park holds out a very thin laptop.
Theo dumps his box of adapters onto the booth desk. Lily starts sorting them with masking tape and a marker.
Lily's masking-tape labels pile up: camera, 2009; phone, not ours; a tiny fan; projector, old.
Maya holds up an adapter in a pool of light, like a trophy. It fits. Theo cheers.
9:14. The slides appear on the screen. Maya brings up the laptop's audio channel, and a low, steady hum fills the room. A waveform shows the program with a steady low wave underneath it.
Maya in the booth, the hum still going. Her first guess: the new adapter is bad. Confidence 60.
Muted: no hum. Unmuted: hum. The hum lives in the laptop's channel.
At the lectern, Maya looks at what the laptop connects to: a charger plugged into the stage outlet, the video adapter to the projector, and the audio cable running back to the booth console.
Gus, a friendly retired congregant who ran sound decades ago, holds out a little plug adapter that drops the round ground pin.

A teaching moment: Ray and Maya beside a board. Hum is the power line singing — sixty hertz here — plus its harmonics: whole-number multiples of it. So the third harmonic is… Three times sixty. One hundred eighty hertz. A ground loop is how the power line gets into your audio cable in the first place.
Maya declines Gus's adapter, kindly.
Close-up: the charger's three-prong plug, fully intact, lies unplugged beside the outlet. The laptop runs on battery at 80 percent. The waveform shows no hum.

System View diagram: the laptop, powered from a stage outlet on one circuit, and the console, powered from a booth outlet on another, are both safely grounded. Their ground references differ slightly, and the audio cable between them carries that difference as hum.
Ray asks Maya what she now thinks. She answers with a confidence of 75.
Ray's drawer: a small box labeled, in his handwriting, ISOLATOR · AUDIO, signal only.
System View again: the same two outlets and circuits, both grounds untouched, with the isolator in the audio cable between the laptop and the console. The audio passes through; the hum does not.
Soundcheck with the charger plugged in and the isolator in the audio line: Maya listens with her eyes closed. The waveform is clean.
9:30, the doors open behind Maya as she writes in her notebook.
10:40. Dr. Park plays her video. The sound comes through the room clearly; the waveform shows no hum underneath.
In the booth, Lily checks the stream on her phone: no hum. Pastor Jo's microphone is clean; the projector picture is fine.
After the service, Dr. Park thanks Maya.
Change log entry #4: 'Guest laptop audio: isolator in the audio line, signal only. No safety ground touched. Request: electrician to check stage versus booth circuits.'
Ray reads the entry. Gus's little adapter sits on the desk beside him, set aside.
Imani, on the phone, books the electrician.
Maya's phone lights up with a text from Sofia: the Easter fixtures have arrived — twelve more lights.

Soundcheck. Lily presses WORSHIP on the touch panel. Marisol sings into her microphone and nothing comes out of the speakers. At the lectern, the pastor's microphone is live and picking up the rustle of pages.
In the booth Maya's first thought: the touch panel is broken. Confidence 70.
Maya talks to Marisol over the radio while watching the console meters: when Marisol sings, channel 7 jumps, not channel 3.
A patch diagram: Marisol's vocal mic and the lectern mic arrive at the patch, but their lines cross — the vocal lands on console channel 7 and the lectern on channel 3.
Theo, who told Maya last week that the tidy-up was happening, comes to the booth.
Change log entry #5, in Mateo's hand: 'Rack tidy — done. Switch moved into rack. — M.' Nothing about the patch.
On Maya's phone, one of Priya's photos from a month ago shows the patch panel with every cable in its original place.
Flashback to Tuesday, from Mateo's point of view. In the equipment room, Mateo is installing a proper rack switch to replace his old TEMP one. His crew member, Kip, tidies the cables.
Close-up flashback: two cables at the patch panel cross each other. Kip unplugs both and swaps them so the lines hang straight. The masking-tape label on one jack has fallen off long ago.
Mateo sees the neat rack and pauses.
Mateo's phone rings: another job has an emergency. He glances at the clipboard.
Flashback, from Imani's point of view: Tuesday at 12:30 she approves the tidy-up on a call with Mateo while Theo listens.
Sunday 9:20, Imani tells Pastor Jo the first song may start two minutes late, and why.
In the equipment room Maya matches the patch to Priya's photo and moves the two cables back, one at a time.
The patch diagram now shows straight lines: Marisol's vocal mic to channel 3, the lectern to channel 7.
Lily presses WORSHIP again. Marisol sings and is heard; the lectern is quiet.
Lily presses every other preset in turn — SPOKEN WORD, BAPTISM, ALL OFF — while Maya watches the right channels open and close.
During the service, the preset changes from worship to the sermon and back: the right microphones open each time.

A teaching moment: Ray and Maya beside a board. Evidence is what you saw or measured, written down before you touch anything. A change record is evidence about what somebody changed. And a label? A label is evidence left for the next person. Worked example: 'MIC 3 → IN 7 · lectern · don't repatch — R.' What it is, where it goes, why it's there.
Mateo comes by in person after the service, finally meeting Maya face to face.
Imani's new one-page checklist: plan the patch in writing; print labels for both ends; log it before you leave; press every preset after; compare to the photos.
Maya teases Ray about his labeled mug. Ray answers deadpan.
Thursday. Mateo, alone in the equipment room, fixes printed labels to both ends of every patch cable.
Sofia, beaming, stands under two new lighting fixtures, pointing at a stack of boxes.
Sofia unpacks new lighting fixtures on the stage while Theo carries boxes.
In the booth, Maya's radio crackles: Theo, reporting a change before he makes it.
Theo looks at the wall outlets by the drums. There's no label on them at all.
Rehearsal. Sofia brings the Easter look up to full: every new fixture blazes. The band plays; Marisol sings.
Half the stage goes dark. The keyboard and the stage-left monitors go silent too.
Pastor Jo, in the half-dark, deadpans.
Imani hurries into the booth. Easter morning is fifteen hours away.
Maya takes charge calmly: lights to zero, people clear.
Maya walks the paths. System View: the stage-left power lane is dark; the booth and the other stage outlets are fine. The lighting console still works; the keyboard is dead only because its power is.
Close-up: the nameplate sticker on the back of a new fixture reads 150 W, 120 V — an example rating. Maya copies it without opening anything.
Maya's load table: 12 new fixtures, 1,800 watts; keyboard and amp, 400; two monitors, 400; pedalboard and miscellaneous, 100; total 2,700 watts. All example numbers from nameplates.

A teaching moment: Ray and Maya beside a board. Current is watts divided by volts. A twelve-hundred-watt heater on a hundred-twenty volts draws ten amps. And the breaker? Plan to eighty percent: a fifteen-amp breaker gives a twelve-amp planning line. The panel is the electrician's. That's a boundary — we bring the numbers, not a screwdriver.

The booth whiteboard: P equals V times I. One example 20-amp circuit at 120 volts: 2,400 watts. They asked for 2,700 watts, which is 22.5 amps. The breaker did its job. Illustrative; the electrician has the real numbers.
Maya explains to Imani why they won't flip the breaker themselves.
Maya on the phone to Andre, the electrician, with her load table in hand.
Andre, on the phone at home.
Andre, a journeyman electrician, and Malik, his apprentice in a hi-vis vest, arrive at the locked electrical room.
Andre unlocks the electrical room and works at the panel. Maya stays outside the taped line; Malik stands ready at the door with Andre's tester.
Malik traces the stage outlets with a circuit tracer under Andre's direction. He sticks small labels on them: C3 on the stage-left wall, C5 on the stage-right wall.
Andre compares Maya's table with what he found.
Malik and Maya talk while Andre finishes at the panel.
10:00 p.m. The full-look test: all twelve fixtures at full and the band playing. Andre's clamp meter reads about 15 amps on circuit 3 — an illustrative reading. Nothing trips for thirty minutes.
Easter morning. The opening look blazes; the room is full. Nothing trips.
In the booth, Lily checks the neighbors: the sound system's circuit is steady, the stream is clean, the keyboard and monitors on circuit 3 work.
After the service, Sofia admits her blind spot.
Change log entry #6: '12 fixtures added (Sofia). C3 overloaded; breaker tripped — it worked as designed. Andre (licensed) moved 6 to C5, labeled stage outlets. Full-look test passed.'
Andre shows Imani the panel's paper schedule taped inside the door.
Ray reads the change-log entry and gives one principle.
Dolores comes to the booth holding an assistive listening receiver.
Dolores in the booth, holding the assistive listening receiver.
Mr. Tunde Adeyemi, another receiver user, waits his turn with the same complaint.
Maya checks a receiver at the booth while the band rehearses. Music comes through clearly.
Tuesday. Maya wears a receiver and has Lily run the service order from the booth: worship, reading, sermon, worship. The receiver goes silent exactly when SPOKEN WORD is pressed.
Lily, at the touch panel, connects it to last month.
Maya's list of every output and who it's for: room speakers, everyone; stream, home; lobby TV, overflow; band wedges, musicians; listening transmitter, receiver users.
In the rack, the listening transmitter's input cable carries a masking-tape label: 'from AUX 4'.

System View: a routing map. The lectern, pastor, vocal and band feed the MAIN bus to the room speakers. AUX 4, the band monitor mix, feeds the band wedges — and, through a dashed line, the listening transmitter. In SPOKEN WORD, AUX 4 is muted, so the transmitter goes silent.

A teaching moment: Ray and Maya beside a board. Feedback is the howl when a mic hears its own speaker. Gain before feedback is how loud you can go before it starts. And more open mics make it worse? By minus ten log of how many more. One mic to four: minus ten times log four — about minus six decibels. Mute what nobody's using.
Ray, reading the same label, remembers.
System View after the fix: a new bus, AUX 6 · LISTENING, takes every speech and music input and feeds only the listening transmitter. It is never muted by any scene.
Avery, an accessibility and user-experience lead Imani knows, arrives to help. They wear lilac and carry a small notebook.
Avery explains how to look at it.
Thursday evening. Dolores in row 8 and Mr. Adeyemi across the aisle, each with a receiver, while Lily steps through every preset and Ana reads a practice scripture passage.
Mr. Adeyemi takes off his receiver and grins.
Dolores gives Avery a note of her own.
Sunday. Ana reads the scripture from the lectern.
In row 8 Dolores listens on her receiver, eyes closed. Maya sits a few seats down with a receiver of her own.
In the booth, Lily checks the neighbors: the room speakers are unchanged, the band wedges stay quiet during the sermon, and the stream is unchanged.
After the service Dolores comes to the booth.
Change log entry #7: 'Listening TX moved off AUX 4 (band monitors) to new AUX 6. Never muted by a scene. Tested with Dolores and Mr. A. in every preset. Monthly: a user walk-test.'
Avery and Imani talk after the debrief.
Ray reads the entry and gives one principle.
Months later: Imani on the phone, a calendar page behind her showing December 24.
The booth. The stream preview monitor shows the LED wall with two dark bands rolling slowly up across it. Theo, on camera 1's headset, looks alarmed. Maya leans in.
The same wall seen from the sanctuary: bright, even, no bands at all. People are finding their seats.
Title card: Three weeks earlier. December 3.
A rented LED wall now fills the back of the stage. Imani introduces Lena, a broadcast engineer from a local studio, wearing a headset around her neck.

A teaching moment: Ray and Maya beside a board. The wall redraws thousands of times a second — its refresh rate. The camera only looks for a sliver of time — its shutter. So how many redraws per look? Refresh times shutter. Three thousand eight hundred forty times one-fiftieth of a second: seventy-six point eight. That point-eight is your stripe.

System View timing diagram before the fix: the wall refreshes at 50 Hz while the camera exposes 59.94 frames per second with an automatic 1/100 shutter. Each frame catches a different slice of the refresh, so the brightness varies from frame to frame and dark bands roll.

System View after the fix: wall input at 59.94 Hz with a refresh that is a whole multiple of it, camera at 59.94 frames per second with a 1/60 shutter. Every frame catches whole refresh cycles; the picture is even.
